intent: Establish a baseline geometry with five evenly spaced, forward-offset sensors covering about twice the tape width, a moderate wheel track and radius for responsive steering, and a light body. Keep the design centred and symmetric so the Integrator can judge the controller without geometry asymmetry. I expect this to complete the development tracks with few line-loss events. I am considering, but not committing to, a narrower sensor spread for sharper tracks, and a larger forward offset if the Integrator reports late reactions.
learning: No race evidence yet. Hypotheses to test: (1) five sensors at 12 mm spacing avoid line loss better than three; (2) forward offset of 40 mm improves rms_error on curves; (3) lighter mass and smaller yaw inertia reduce oscillation. Next iteration, I will check which of these the race data supports.
rationale: This is the first iteration, so there is no Integration Feedback or Geometry Race Data yet and nothing to adopt or reject. I am starting from a neutral baseline built from the contract. Five sensors at 12 mm spacing (x = -0.024 to +0.024 m) span about 48 mm, roughly twice the 25 mm tape width. That gives a continuous read across the line, so the controller can keep a signal through bends and small errors without losing the line. The sensors sit 40 mm ahead of the axle, which gives look-ahead so the robot turns before the tape reaches the wheels. The 12 mm footprint is a middle choice: it is large enough to avoid dead zones between sensors and small enough to keep the signal sharp. Track width 0.12 m and wheel radius 0.03 m give a moderate turn-rate response and a speed that can reach the roughly 1.5 m/s needed to finish within 3 s. Mass 0.8 kg and body length 0.16 m keep yaw inertia low enough for quick corrections. Body width 0.14 m keeps the off-track limit at its 0.06 m floor, so it does not widen the allowed error. I expect a completed run on the development tracks with few line-loss events, with the main risk being overshoot on the sharpest bend. I have not yet tested whether the wider spread or the forward offset helps.
